text: Friday, four in the morning. Out at sea, Kanghan's barge is lit up like a stadium.
With two days left on the lid, Geum orders him to stop carrying. It sounds insane, until she names the replacement.
Then she invites Borro to hit her with everything. Borro, a gentle giant, needs that confirmed.
He slams his iron shield into her ladle. The concrete cracks under her slippers. She doesn't move.
And the force doesn't go anywhere. It stays in the ladle, humming.
Then she turns and taps a tetrapod the size of a car, and it splits clean in two.
Pim shrieks his summary of events. Technically it was concrete and a ladle, but the point stands.
This is how the Wall of Busan got her name. Not by hitting harder than everything else.
Jaeha names her old S-rank skill. Geum corrects the tense, and taps the steel arm that hasn't forgotten.
Jaeha sees the difference. PASS hands a hit straight on, losing some. Hers waits for orders.
So he drags up PASS's terms. Clause three: force passing between bodies can stop in him. Risk: his bones.
Jaeha smiles like a man who's found a loophole.
First try. Geum strikes Borro's shield, and Jaeha catches the force instead of passing it on.
He can't hold it. It bursts out through his hand, and his finger bends the wrong way.
Geum checks her watch. No sympathy, just a schedule built round Borro's cooldown.
The splint is a chopstick and tape. Geum's bedside manner matches her training.
At six, out at sea, the barge starts to drill.
Every boom makes Pim wince. Whatever is under the lid likes it even less.
Jaeha plans the day in a left-handed scrawl. Four chances, if his bones allow.
Eight o'clock. Second try. This time the glow stays in his chest.
He's done this before, in a wheelchair, with a cup. Set one was this lesson all along.
It earns a name. Store, level one: three seconds, and a warning about his bones.
Then he lays his palm on Borro's shield and gives the hit back with a soft thud, grinning through a nosebleed.
At noon he holds it for ten seconds, his whole arm glowing, his bones creaking.
Pim hears the lid weakening with every boom. The deadline is moving up.
Lyra wants eyes on the drilling. It's far past LINK's range, but Lyra is river-folk.
So at one-thirty, a little fishing boat chugs out toward the barge, riding very low with Borro aboard.
It belongs to the old fisherman Jaeha saved on Tuesday night, repaying him with a day at sea.
Five hundred metres off, a loudhailer turns them away, and Han Sora waves from the rail like a hostess.
Lyra steps onto the gunwale in field form and her river-blue bikini, perfectly aware of her audience.
She dives straight down.
Pim opens his wings at the bow and becomes her navigator, his voice reaching down through the water.
Through the link, Jaeha sees the lid: stone and steel too wide to see the edge of, Kanghan's new anchor bolts drilled in.
And a crack spreading out from the drill holes, with violet light seeping through.
So much for Hwang's reinforcing. Geum grips the gunwale while her steel arm twitches.
Below the crack the violet lantern glows, something vast turning past it. Lyra's hand drifts toward the light. Pim shouts her back.
Forty seconds of field form left, and she's still thirty metres down.
She bursts out onto the barge's fender, right under Sora, and blows her a kiss with a critique of the engineering.
Troopers come running, but Sora just admires the performance.
Back in the boat, Lyra is shivering, the smile gone. Jaeha hands her a towel, eyes on the sky. He felt that pull too.
At four, Moon Ahin does what nobody else can: she calls the Director himself, as family.
He answers with the same question he asked her in Seoul. Only the city has changed.
She hangs up on him.
On the breakwater, Jaeha holds Borro's blocked hit for thirty seconds, glowing from his chest to his fingertips.
Out at sea, the lid has lost another two percent. Thirty hours to go.
At six-forty, a girl with a school backpack walks up the harbour road.
It's Seoa, straight off the train. If her brother can't come home for Friday dinner, dinner comes to him.
Then the two scariest women in his life size each other up, arms folded the same way.
And they bow to each other at the exact same moment. Instant mutual respect.
Jaeha realises he will never win an argument again.
Seoa finds the chopstick taped to his finger, and his explanation is one word long.
Six fifty-eight. Everyone squeezes round the counter, even Moon Ahin, gloves off, and Seoa runs the table.
The clock ticks to six fifty-nine.
Out on the barge, an engineer punches the air, and the anchor team runs for the launchers.
And violet light bursts up out of the seabed under the barge.
Pim's chopsticks clatter, his headset sliding off. He knows that sound.
The lid's clock collapses from more than a day to under an hour.
Geum's steel fist clenches on its own, and she picks up her ladle.
Around the counter, everyone has turned toward the sea. Seoa grips her brother's sleeve.
Geum stands with the ladle on her shoulder and a grim, crooked grin. Seven o'clock will have to wait.
